source_refs.note: Topic 1.7.1, printed pages 7-8: atomic radius and its trends (Figure 1.4).

blocks.text: The atomic radius is a measure of the size of an atom: half the distance between two identical atoms bonded together. It can vary with the type of bond (covalent, metallic or van der Waals) or the state of the atom; the radius in a covalent bond differs from that in an ionic bond. It is measured in picometres (pm) or angstroms.

The factors affecting the atomic radius are the atomic number, the effective nuclear charge and the shielding effect of the inner electrons. Generally the atomic radius decreases across a period from left to right, because the increasing nuclear charge pulls the electron cloud closer. Conversely it increases down a group, because additional electron shells are added and more shielding makes the atom larger even though the nuclear charge also rises, which is outweighed.

blocks.alt: Left: a row of blue circles from lithium to fluorine shrinking to the right, and a column of pink circles from lithium to rubidium growing downward, with arrows and notes. Right: a sodium atom beside a smaller sodium ion, and a chlorine atom beside a larger chloride ion, with notes on cations, anions and isoelectronic series.
blocks.caption: Atomic radius across a period and down a group, and ionic radius against the atom (original diagram after Figures 1.4 and 1.5; circles are schematic).
blocks.long_description: Across period 2 the atoms shrink from lithium to fluorine because the nuclear charge rises while the electrons stay in the same shell; down group 1 the atoms grow from lithium to rubidium because each element adds a shell and the inner electrons shield the outer ones. A cation such as sodium ion is smaller than its atom because the lost electrons leave less repulsion, and an anion such as chloride is larger than its atom because the gained electrons add repulsion. Both kinds of ion shrink across a period and grow down a group.
